Text

English uses the spelling you picked from the strip or typed on a keyboard. A word written only by its sounds shows its English when exactly one word has those sounds; a word that shares its sounds with another (see, sea), or sounds that make no word, come out as sounds between slashes. Pasting English into this keyboard brings back the Stemsyl, and a backup file keeps everything.

View and paste

Under each word
Glyph size
Paste English

You can also paste straight onto the page. Each word becomes its sounds; a word that isn’t in the word list is skipped, and you can spell it with the keys.

Consonants — colour is the family, up · centred · down

Up voiceless · centred the family’s sonorant · down voiced. The families run round the colour wheel from the tongue tip to the back of the mouth, so a misread lands on a related sound.

Vowels — colour is the vowel, centred · up · down

The vowels take six rainbow colours plus grey, two each: red a · eye, orange ah · ow, yellow e · ay, green i · ee, blue u · oo, grey uh · aw, violet oh · oy. Centred is the plain vowel, up glides to i, down glides to u.

How the keys work

Every key is one sound. The note groups the sounds of a word into syllables by itself: each vowel takes the consonant just before it on its left and the one just after it on its right. Any other consonant stands on a short stub of its own.

After the sounds of a word, the strip above the keys offers the English words that sound like it, and longer words that begin with it. When exactly one English word has the sounds you wrote, its spelling goes under the glyphs and into Copy English by itself. Words that share their sounds with another (see, sea; to, two, too) stay as sounds until you tap one — except eye alone, which is always I, and uh alone, which is always a. After the ◆ name mark, names count too, so Jon and John wait for your choice. Tapping a longer word finishes the word; the note itself shows only the sounds.

The ◆ key is the name mark: it goes before a name, where English uses a capital letter. Numerals are dice on a 3 × 3 grid — count the lit squares.

There are two layouts, switched at the top of the keyboard. Keys has a key for every sound. 3 × 3 asks for a tick position first, then its colour; hold its centre for numbers, punctuation and cursor keys, and swipe sideways across it to move the cursor.

Typing on a physical keyboard

Type English. Each word turns into its sounds when you press space, Enter or a punctuation key. A capital letter in the middle of a sentence adds the name mark. Digits type numerals. Arrows move the cursor; ⌘/Ctrl-Z undoes.

Word data and licences

This app is free software: you can share and change it under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or later, and it comes with no warranty. Its word list is also offered on its own under CC BY-SA 4.0, and the Stemsyl writing system itself is dedicated to the public domain (CC0 1.0), so anyone may use, teach and build on it.

Words: every word of the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary and of the English Speller Database’s American list at size 80 — 271,173 in all. Pronunciations (General American, written in Stemsyl sounds): 117,746 from the CMU dictionary; 102,503 built from those by regular endings, prefixes and compounds (abjured from abjure, aboveground from above and ground); and 50,924 rarer words and names predicted by eSpeak NG (GPL-3.0), with a second guess from Kyubyong Park and Jongseok Kim’s g2p model (Apache-2.0) where the two nearly agree. Predicted pronunciations are usually right or one sound off.

Word order: Hermit Dave’s FrequencyWords, counted from OpenSubtitles 2018 and licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Words it never counted follow, the commoner speller lists first. Offensive words are kept out of the longer-word suggestions, partly using the LDNOOBW list (CC BY 4.0); they can still be written by their sounds.
